summary: SANARE Espacial is health monitoring software for astronauts on long missions, far from any hospital. During months of travel, the crew faces radiation, bone mass loss, cardiovascular changes, sleep disorders, and loss of motor coordination, with the medical team hundreds or thousands of kilometers away. Our solution connects the crew member’s smartwatch to the platform and tracks vital signs and radiation dose in real time. On board, the astronaut receives step-by-step clinical guidance, with voice, and a locator for kits and supplies. In ground control, the team sees ECG, SpO₂, blood pressure, and EtCO₂, sends ready-made procedures, and draws over the image to guide the care. We use NASA’s open data (Human Research Program, ISS dosimetry on OSDR) to define what to measure and the reference ranges. The prototype runs on synthetic sources, and the next step is to use real mission data. SANARE ends the distance: more connection, care, and control.
details:
Sanare Espacial is a web-based aerospace telemedicine platform developed to explore remote monitoring of crew members’ health and to support communication between on-board teams and medical professionals on the ground. The project is part of the Sanare ecosystem, which also has a terrestrial clinical care environment.

In the space interface, the operator selects a crew member and starts a virtual connection with their monitoring device. They then access a dashboard with individual data on heart rate, electrocardiogram, oxygen saturation, blood pressure, respiratory rate, and capnography. The platform also presents cabin environmental information and a personal dosimetry panel, with absorbed dose rate and accumulated radiation exposure. In the current version, these measurements are generated by simulation, without connection to physical sensors.

The system offers step-by-step guided instructions, voice features, location of equipment in the cabin, supply control, and visual annotations to support communication. It also allows representing latency and signal loss scenarios, keeping actions in local queues for later processing. These features make it possible to study how the interface behaves under connectivity limitations and situations of higher operational load.

The intended benefits include centralizing health information, making it easier to identify changes in the monitored parameters, reducing the fragmentation of information, and making the interaction between crew members and support teams clearer. The expected impact is to contribute to research, demonstrations, and evaluations of interfaces for medical assistance in remote environments, including aerospace applications and hard-to-reach terrestrial locations.

The development uses React, TypeScript, Vite, Tailwind CSS, Shadcn/ui components, and Lucide icons. The biomedical charts are rendered with HTML5 Canvas; state management uses Zustand, and local persistence uses IndexedDB with Dexie.js. The terrestrial ecosystem uses Amazon AWS for authentication and database services. The application works in computer, tablet, and smartphone browsers, without requiring specialized hardware.

The creative aspect lies in the combination of biomedical monitoring, radiation exposure, environmental context, and guided assistance in an integrated interface. The development decisions considered legibility, contrast, responsiveness, differences between crew member profiles, accessibility, limited connectivity, and support for American English, Spanish, and Portuguese.
dataRefs: Evaluating the Medical Kit System  for the International Space Station   A Paradigm Revisited
